metaDesc: A cross-province plan linking Samut Prakan and Bangkok: see Pak Nam, the Ancient City and Phra Chulachomklao Fort, then ride the BTS Green Line into the capital. A 2-day, 1-night trip done entirely by train.

ogTitle: Samut Prakan–Bangkok Trip: Pak Nam Then Into the City
ogDesc: A 2-day, 1-night trip through Pak Nam and on into Bangkok by BTS Green Line, mapped out hour by hour for each day.
intro: The nice thing about Pak Nam is that it basically blends into Bangkok already. The BTS Green Line runs straight from the city out to its last stop at Kheha Samut Prakan, so you can spend a day on the coast and around the old temples on the Pak Nam side, then ride the train into the capital the next day without ever driving yourself. Here's a 2-day, 1-night plan with the whole route mapped out for you.

blocks.html: Most people write off Pak Nam as just somewhere you pass through, but you can actually fill a whole day here without going far. And once you've had your fill of the coast and old temples, you just walk up to the BTS station and ride into Bangkok to wander Sukhumvit, Yaowarat, or catch the sunset along the Chao Phraya. This trip is built around the train as the main backbone, with short hops by songthaew and taxi to fill in the spots the BTS doesn't reach.

blocks.text: Why pair Samut Prakan with Bangkok

blocks.html: The Green Line's Bearing–Kheha Samut Prakan extension has 9 stations, running from the Bangkok side inward: Samrong · Pu Chao · Chang Erawan · Royal Thai Naval Academy · Pak Nam · Srinagarindra · Phraeksa · Sai Luat · Kheha (the terminus). That means almost all of Pak Nam's main sights sit along this line, so you can stitch it into one seamless trip with Bangkok.

items: Chang Erawan Station — get off right at the Erawan Museum (the three-headed elephant); it's walkable.
Pak Nam Station — the heart of the old town, Pak Nam Market, and the ferry pier across to Phra Samut Chedi are all close by.
Kheha Station — the end of the line; connect by songthaew to the Ancient City, Crocodile Farm, Bang Pu, and Phra Chula Fort.

blocks.title: BTS fares
blocks.html: The Samut Prakan extension charges fares separately from the main line, so if you're hitting several stations in one day, topping up a Rabbit card beforehand is easier than buying single tokens trip by trip. Check the last train of the day too — the final service from the end of the line usually runs around midnight.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Cover Pak Nam in full: coast, temples, food

blocks.html: The first day stays entirely on the Samut Prakan side. Start at the farthest point (out by the river mouth), then work your way back toward the old town, finishing at Pak Nam Market in the evening when the food choices are at their best.

items.activity: Take the BTS to Kheha, the last stop, then grab a taxi or songthaew to Phra Chulachomklao Fort.
items.note: A Rama V-era fort right at the river mouth, with the warship HTMS Mae Klong on display to climb aboard. Free entry, and it opens early when crowds are thin and the sun isn't fierce yet.

items.activity: Double back to the Ancient City (Muang Boran).
items.note: An open-air museum recreating historic sites from all over Thailand across more than 800 rai. Rent a bike or golf cart to get around, and set aside at least 2–3 hours.

items.activity: Have lunch near the Ancient City, then head back into town via Pak Nam Station.
items.note: For this leg, take songthaew route 36 or a taxi back to the BTS.

items.activity: Take the cross-river ferry from Pak Nam Market over to Phra Samut Chedi on the far bank.
items.note: The ferry costs just a few baht. The chedi is a landmark paired with the town, and on the way back you catch the river views once the sun softens.

items.activity: Eat your way through Pak Nam Market in the evening.
items.note: Loads of old-school vendors here — Je Juk yentafo, Hia Pee fish-ball noodles, the late-night oyster omelet, and Ngam Ta's frozen-yolk coconut ice cream over in Trok Hoi.

blocks.title: Where to stay tonight
blocks.html: Pick a hotel around Pak Nam or Srinagarindra station so you can wake up and hop on the BTS into Bangkok the next morning with the shortest walk. Check the options we've gathered on our Top 10 Samut Prakan hotels page.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Ride the Green Line into Bangkok

blocks.html: Day two shifts the focus into Bangkok. From Pak Nam, hop on the same BTS line straight into Sukhumvit without changing trains — you can shop Siam, walk Asok–Thonglor, or carry on toward the Chao Phraya, whatever you like. We've laid this out as a day of walking, eating, and shopping, wrapping up by the river in the evening.

items.activity: Check out and take the BTS from Pak Nam Station heading into the city.
items.note: Ride the Green Line straight into Sukhumvit, no transfers needed. It takes about 50–60 minutes to reach the Asok/Siam area.

items.activity: Get off at Siam–Chidlom for malls, shopping, and cafés.
items.note: The malls here connect via elevated skywalks, so even when the sun's blazing you can walk indoors the whole way.

items.activity: Lunch around Asok–Thonglor, or get off at Sukhumvit and find a spot you like.
items.note: If you want bold street food, it's worth riding the MRT on to Yaowarat in the late afternoon.

items.activity: Head toward Saphan Taksin and catch the Chao Phraya Express Boat.
items.note: Ride the BTS to Saphan Taksin Station, then take a boat to IconSiam or Tha Tien to see Wat Arun and Wat Pho along the river.

items.activity: Watch the sunset over the Chao Phraya to close out the trip.
items.note: Pick a riverside spot or a rooftop around Charoen Krung/Khlong San for a farewell dinner before everyone heads off.

blocks.text: Must-try food on both sides of the trip

blocks.html: The charm of this plan is getting two food styles in one trip. The Pak Nam side leans on fresh seafood and long-running market vendors, while the Bangkok side spans everything from mall cafés to Yaowarat street food. Here are the spots Pak Nam locals talk about most.

items.name: Je Juk Yentafo
items.blurb: The famous yentafo nearly every Pak Nam local recommends — bold red broth, generous toppings, right in the Pak Nam Market area and walkable from the BTS.

items.name: Hia Pee Noodles (longtime shop)
items.blurb: House-made fish balls with a real bounce in a clear broth — a place that always lands near the top of locals' lists for the neighborhood.

items.name: Late-Night Oyster Omelet (longtime shop)
items.blurb: An oyster omelet made with duck egg as its signature — crisp on the outside, soft inside, open late into the night. A good stop after browsing the market.

items.name: Ngam Ta Frozen-Yolk Ice Cream (Trok Hoi)
items.blurb: An old-school coconut-milk ice cream in Trok Hoi — dense, just the right sweetness, a market-style dessert to finish off a savory meal.
items.meta: Trok Hoi, Pak Nam Market · dessert

items.name: Fresh seafood at Pak Nam Market
items.blurb: Pak Nam is an old fishing port, so the market is a source for shrimp, shellfish, crab, and fish at good prices, with several stalls cooking it up fresh.

items.name: Yaowarat Street Food (Bangkok side)
items.blurb: Worth a stop on day two — take the MRT from Sukhumvit to Yaowarat in the evening and eat your way down the street: grilled seafood, noodles, and desserts.

blocks.text: Want some nature? Stop by Bang Krachao

blocks.html: If you've got time to spare or want to add another half-day of green, Bang Krachao sits on the Phra Pradaeng side, right between Pak Nam and Bangkok. It's a pig-stomach-shaped green lung in a bend of the Chao Phraya, and the usual move is to ferry across and ride a bike along the raised paths that wind through orchards and canal-side communities.

items.name: Ferry from Wat Bang Na Nok pier
items.blurb: On the Bang Na side there's a ferry that takes bikes too, costing just a few baht per person. Once across, you can rent a bike for the whole day for around 80 THB.

items.name: Bang Nam Phueng Floating Market
items.blurb: Open only Saturday–Sunday, late morning into the afternoon, with local snacks and souvenirs. If you want to stop by, plan the trip to land on a weekend.

blocks.title: Timing worth knowing
blocks.html: Bang Nam Phueng Floating Market is only open Saturday–Sunday, and the Ancient City eats up more time than you'd expect. If you want both in one trip, save Bang Krachao for a weekend and cover the Ancient City and coast on another day — it works out better that way.

faq.q: Can I do Samut Prakan and then Bangkok without a car?
faq.a: Easily. The BTS Green Line runs straight from Kheha Samut Prakan into Sukhumvit in central Bangkok with no transfers. Main sights like Chang Erawan and Pak Nam Market are right by the stations, while the Ancient City, Crocodile Farm, and Phra Chula Fort are a short songthaew or taxi hop from the end of the line.

faq.q: How many days does this trip need?
faq.a: Two days and one night is just right. Day one covers the Pak Nam side — coast, old temples, and the Ancient City — with a night near Pak Nam Station. Day two rides the BTS into Bangkok to walk, eat, and shop, finishing along the Chao Phraya. If you want to add Bang Krachao, stretch it to three days.

faq.q: Which BTS station is for the Ancient City and Phra Chula Fort?
faq.a: Both are near Kheha, the last station. Get off the BTS and continue by songthaew route 36 or taxi for the final stretch. Phra Chula Fort sits right at the river mouth and is free to enter, while the Ancient City has an entry fee and a very large area — set aside 2–3 hours.

faq.q: If I want to add Bang Krachao, which day should I go?
faq.a: If you're set on walking through Bang Nam Phueng Floating Market, you'll need to go Saturday or Sunday since that's the only time it's open. To cross over to Bang Krachao, the usual route is the ferry from Wat Bang Na Nok pier on the Bang Na side, then rent a bike to ride around the bend.

faq.q: What Pak Nam food should I try?
faq.a: It's known for fresh seafood at Pak Nam Market. As for the longtime shops locals recommend, there's Je Juk yentafo, Hia Pee fish-ball noodles, the late-night duck-egg oyster omelet, and Ngam Ta's frozen-yolk ice cream over in Trok Hoi.
